clue.text: That bloke with a cast bearing left for transport hub

parts.note: an air is a manner or bearing
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A man with his arm in plaster making his way to a busy terminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the pieces; 'cast' looks like a plaster cast but is the verb throw, and 'bearing' is the noun air, as in an air of confidence.
explanation.definitionFit: The London airport is one of the busiest travel interchanges in the world, a hub for flights.

clue.text: Swimmer remarks he had ham, surprisingly

indicators.note: something that happens surprisingly comes out in an unexpected way, so the letters land in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A swimmer comments, to everyone's astonishment, on having eaten ham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' reads like a person at the pool, but crosswords often use it for any fish.
explanation.definitionFit: This fish with a flattened, mallet-shaped head is a creature that lives and moves in water, so a swimmer.

clue.text: Singers regularly wail, at worst

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept and the rest are skipped

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A complaint about vocalists who, at their worst, simply wail.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the comma and the word breaks: take every second letter of the run of letters starting from the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Altos are vocalists with a low female or high male voice part in a choir.

clue.text: Noses about excessively, probing quiet revolutionary

indicators.note: a revolution turns things right round, so the whole assembly is read backwards
a probe pushes inside something, so one piece goes into another

explanation.surface: Nosy people poking about too much in a silent rebel's business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noses about' reads as prying, but 'Noses' alone is the definition, and 'revolutionary' is not a rebel but a signal that turns the whole assembly round.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooter is informal British slang for a nose, especially a large one.

clue.text: Adjusts to siren going off

indicators.note: something going off has exploded or gone bad, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone gets used to an alarm sounding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' looks like a link word joining 'Adjusts' to the rest, but its letters belong in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To orient something is to position or align it correctly, which is a way of adjusting it.

clue.text: Draw area of land to the south of Aldershot's borders

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece to the south sits lower, so it comes later in the word
the borders of a word are its edges, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the town's name
a tract is an expanse of land

explanation.surface: Sketching a plot of land below the Hampshire army town of Aldershot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' suggests sketching a map, but it means to pull in. Aldershot is a garrison town in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a crowd is to attract it, pulling people towards something; the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Ask sappers to lead mission

indicators.note: whatever leads goes in front, so this piece comes first

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, whose soldiers are called sappers
a quest is a mission or search

explanation.surface: Asking army engineers to take charge of an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: Sappers are military engineers; in the British Army they serve in the Royal Engineers, abbreviated RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ask for something is to make a formal plea for it; the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Work in theatre, helping to support old people on vacation

indicators.note: in a down answer a support sits underneath, so this piece comes after the other
a word on vacation has emptied out, leaving only its outside letters

parts.note: the word with its middle cleared out
a helping is a portion or ration

explanation.surface: A care worker in a theatre, helping elderly people who are away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre is the operating theatre, not the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgery performed in a hospital's operating room is the work done there by the surgeon.

clue.text: Magazine article says chap gets hold of novel

indicators.note: to get hold of something is to grasp it, so one part closes around another

parts.note: novel as an adjective means new

explanation.surface: A magazine piece reports that a man has acquired a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Magazine article' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'Magazine'. The novel is not a book but an adjective, slotted in after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: This British weekly political and cultural periodical has been published in London since 1913.

clue.text: Protestant satisfied with raise, receiving old penny

parts.note: a demand that is met has been satisfied

indicators.note: whatever receives something takes it in, so one piece is placed inside

parts.note: d was the symbol for the pre-decimal British penny

explanation.surface: A churchgoer content with a pay rise that includes an outdated coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise' looks like a pay rise but is the verb, giving HOIST, which then holds the D.
explanation.definitionFit: Methodism is a Protestant denomination founded by John Wesley, so its members are Protestants.

clue.text: Perhaps waiters signal audibly

definitions.note: plural people defining a single noun for a line of them

indicators.note: something done audibly is heard, so the word is taken by its spoken form

parts.note: a cue is a signal to act

explanation.surface: Restaurant staff perhaps giving a call out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waiters' suggests restaurant staff, but here they are just people waiting, and 'Perhaps' warns that this is a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A line of people standing and waiting their turn is made up of those who wait.

clue.text: Festival not primarily from India?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is kept

explanation.surface: Asking whether a festival is really of Indian origin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not primarily' looks like a deletion, but it takes the first letter of 'not'. The question mark marks India as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: India lies in the East, so something originating there is oriental; the question mark admits it is an example.

clue.text: Indifferent, assert how old you are?

parts.note: your age is how old you are

explanation.surface: Someone, unbothered, being asked to state their age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indifferent' suggests not caring, but it is used in its other sense of neither good nor bad.
explanation.definitionFit: Indifferent can mean mediocre, of only middling quality, which is ordinary or so-so.

clue.text: Turning around to some extent elicits involuntary movement

indicators.note: something turned around faces the other way, so the letters are read backwards
only part of the text is used, so the letters sit inside a word

parts.note: the middle letters of the word

explanation.surface: Twisting round can partly provoke a twitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning around' looks like the movement itself but tells you to read the run of letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tic is a sudden repeated twitch, usually in the face, that a person cannot control.

clue.text: Vehicles pick up seeds periodically

parts.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it

indicators.note: at regular periods, so every other letter is kept

explanation.surface: Trucks collecting a scattering of seed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick up' suggests collecting by vehicle, but it means catching a sound.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the long cars that carry coffins to funerals, a particular kind of motor transport.

clue.text: Blair made changes deserving respect

indicators.note: making changes alters an arrangement, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Tony Blair, the former British prime minister, earns credit for reforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' does double duty: its letters join the mix while 'made changes' also reads as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worthy of esteem or praise is admirable; the phrase is a straight synonym.

clue.text: Zeus's wife missing husband for some time

indicators.note: something missing has gone, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: the queen of the Greek gods

explanation.surface: A goddess whose husband has been absent for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures Zeus himself as the missing husband; in fact H is the abbreviation removed from HERA.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a lengthy period of history, so a stretch of time.

clue.text: Spuds from Scotland almost as cheap as can be

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut

parts.note: tatty means cheap and shabby; this is its superlative

explanation.surface: Scottish potatoes sold at rock-bottom prices.
explanation.walkthrough: Spuds is British slang for potatoes, and tatties is the Scots word for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatties is the Scottish colloquial term for potatoes, exactly what the regional label asks for.

clue.text: Notice Oscar in trouble

parts.note: an ad is a notice or advertisement
O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Spotting that Oscar has got into difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a container signal but just joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ado is fuss or bother, as in Much Ado About Nothing, which is a form of difficulty.

clue.text: Lacking boundaries, call Omani back for annual publication

indicators.note: without its boundaries a word loses its edges, keeping only its inner letters

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters
the word without its first and last letters
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Freely phoning a man from Oman to get hold of a yearly book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' wants to be a reversal signal, but it is simply the third word to lose its edges.
explanation.definitionFit: An almanac is a book issued every year containing a calendar and astronomical or seasonal information.

clue.text: Lack of experience from any vet, I suspect

indicators.note: something suspect is dodgy or not right, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Someone suspects an animal doctor of being green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' reads as a verb with 'I', but it is an adjective telling you the letters are wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Naivety is innocence and unworldliness, the state of someone who has not yet learned much.

clue.text: In Madagascar, I bought deer

indicators.note: the answer is inside the words that follow, running across them

parts.note: the run starts near the end of the island's name

explanation.surface: A traveller buys an animal while visiting the island of Madagascar.
explanation.walkthrough: There are no deer in Madagascar, which is a hint the place name is only there to supply letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The caribou is the North American reindeer, a large species of the family Cervidae.

clue.text: European cheers, having eaten new maize porridge

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside the eater, so one piece is placed within

parts.note: a Pole is a person from Poland

explanation.surface: A European raising a toast after a meal of cornmeal mush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' is British slang for thanks, not a toast. The new letter is eaten by the European and the thanks together, landing between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Polenta is an Italian dish of boiled cornmeal, a thick porridge made from corn.

clue.text: Extremely profane policeman arrests sailor, causing fireworks

indicators.note: to arrest someone is to take them in, so one piece is held inside
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those are kept

explanation.surface: A foul-mouthed officer nicks a seaman, and sparks fly.
explanation.walkthrough: The ends of 'profane' and the policeman's DS together form one container that holds the sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A petard is a small explosive device, now also a kind of firecracker, as in hoist with his own petard.

clue.text: German rock singer learning line that is coming up

parts.note: lore is learning or traditional knowledge

indicators.note: in a down answer, something coming up rises from bottom to top, so it reads backwards

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation for that is

explanation.surface: A German rock vocalist rehearsing an upcoming lyric.
explanation.walkthrough: The rock is not music: the Lorelei is a rock on the Rhine, home in legend to a siren whose song lured boatmen to their deaths.
explanation.definitionFit: In Rhine legend she is a maiden who sat on a cliff by the river and sang sailors to their doom.

clue.text: A&E collecting X-ray tool

indicators.note: to collect something is to gather it in, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: the letters of the hospital department's name
X in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Casualty picking up a scanning device.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E is the British hospital accident and emergency department. X-ray is not a scan here but the radio code word for X.
explanation.definitionFit: An axe is an implement for chopping wood, a standard cutting tool.

clue.text: Introduction to bodybuilding leaves son sturdier and more grumpy

indicators.note: whatever leaves departs, so that letter is taken away
an introduction is the very start, so only the opening letter is taken

explanation.surface: Starting weight training leaves a young man beefier and crankier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' looks like a verb of departing from the gym, and it is: the B departs from BURLIER, which follows S.
explanation.definitionFit: Surly means bad-tempered and unfriendly, so its comparative means more bad-tempered.

clue.text: Call that thing English insect

parts.note: to call something is to name or term it

explanation.surface: Naming a bug found in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call' reads as a phone call or a shout but here means to name.
explanation.definitionFit: A termite is a small social insect that lives in colonies and eats wood.

clue.text: Fool One Direction to start with — it takes nothing

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside another
what comes to start with is the very beginning, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A dig at the boy band One Direction for being dimwits from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: One Direction is a pop group, but here the two words are split into I and D.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiot is a stupid person, the same as a fool; the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Walk better unclothed

indicators.note: with its clothes off, a word is stripped of its outer layer, so first and last letters go

parts.note: a better is one who bets

explanation.surface: Strolling is improved when done naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' looks like the comparative of good, but it is a noun: a person who bets.
explanation.definitionFit: To amble is to walk at a slow, relaxed and leisurely pace, so it is a gentle stroll.

clue.text: Desperately bully emir to get metal

indicators.note: acting desperately is acting wildly and chaotically, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: Leaning hard on an oil-rich ruler to secure a mineral resource.
explanation.walkthrough: Note the spelling: the double L and the Y come from 'bully'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beryllium is a light, hard grey chemical element, number four in the periodic table.

clue.text: On tour, hire pesky cooks — don't get mad!

indicators.note: to cook something is to alter or falsify it, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Advice not to lose your temper with annoying chefs hired on a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooks' looks like the chefs themselves, but it is a verb telling you to rework the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal idiom urges someone to calm down and stop being angry.
